title: Influence of Post-Combustion Pressures (from 50 Bar to 350 Bar) Under Three Rocket Liquid Propellant Fuels: Liquid Hydrogen (LH2), Liquid Methane (CH4), and Rocket Propellant-1 (RP-1)
content: In liquid propellant rocket propulsion, the absolute chamber pressure is one of the parameters for preliminary design. In the current study, we quantify the impact of this rocket design parameter (the chamber pressure) on various combustion and nozzle characteristics for three common liquid fuels, which are (1) liquid hydrogen (LH2), (2) liquid methane (CH4), and (3) Rocket Propellant-1 (RP-1), when used with liquid oxygen (LOX) as an oxidizer. The area-to-throat ratio was set to a reasonable value of 10. The range of absolute chamber pressure varies from a low level of 50 bar to a very high level of 350 bar, which allows exploration of rocket performance not typically available in the literature. Twelve properties were computed over this wide range of combustion pressure, which are (1) characteristic velocity, (2) exhaust molecular weight, (3) exhaust isentropic exponent, (4) chamber temperature, (5) exhaust absolute pressure, (6) chamber-to-exit pressure ratio, (7) exhaust temperature, (8) exhaust density, (9) exhaust Mach number, (10) rocket-relative exhaust velocity, (11) ideal specific impulse, and (12) thrust coefficient. The findings of the study show that liquid hydrogen consistently gives much higher exhaust velocity and specific impulse than liquid methane, which is mildly better than RP-1. Also, the results show that the combustion pressure impact is weak for the exhaust molecular weight, rocket-relative exhaust velocity, ideal specific impulse, and characteristic velocity. Increasing the chamber pressure monotonically increases the exhaust isentropic exponent, chamber temperature, exhaust absolute pressure, chamber-to-exit pressure ratio, exhaust temperature, exhaust density, and exhaust Mach number. On the other hand, increasing the chamber pressure monotonically decreases the thrust coefficient.
